title: Majestic Geometry
summary: Attack the bishop before taking the rook, then use checking rook sacrifices to make promotion decisive.

nodes.question: Why is taking the rook not enough?
nodes.explanation: The bishop on d5 can recapture a promoted piece on g8. White first needs to disrupt that diagonal.

branches.title: Drive the king onto the bishop’s rank
commentary: Begin after ...Rg8. Taking that rook immediately would leave only a drawn rook-versus-bishop ending.
Rd4 attacks the bishop and keeps the threat hxg8=Q. In this exact position it is the only winning move.
Be6 stays on the diagonal to g8, preparing to capture a promoted queen.
Rd7+ sacrifices the rook with check, forcing Black to address its king before saving the diagonal arrangement.
Ka8 is the illustrated back-rank retreat. The king now shares the eighth rank with the bishop’s future square.
hxg8=Q captures the rook and promotes. This time the location of Black’s king changes the liquidation.
Bxg8 removes the new queen but places the bishop on the king’s rank.
Rd8+ checks Ka8 and attacks Bg8 along the same rank. White wins the bishop after the king moves; the exact endpoint is winning.
branches.explanation: Rd8+ checks Ka8 and attacks Bg8 along the same rank. White wins the bishop after the king moves; the exact endpoint is winning.

branches.title: Use a checking sacrifice against ...Bb3
commentary: Compare the other illustrated bishop retreat that keeps control of g8.
Rd4 attacks the bishop before committing the pawn.
Bb3 continues to defend g8 along b3-c4-d5-e6-f7-g8.
Ra4+ offers the rook with check. Taking it would abandon the promotion diagonal; moving the king permits a different fork.
Kb7 is the source’s selected king response.
Rb4+ checks Kb7 up the b-file while attacking Bb3 below the rook. White keeps a checked win; other king replies are not enumerated here.
branches.explanation: Rb4+ checks Kb7 up the b-file while attacking Bb3 below the rook. White keeps a checked win; other king replies are not enumerated here.

branches.title: The bishop accepts the checking rook offer
commentary: The checking sacrifice also works if Black accepts it.
Rd4 attacks the bishop and prepares the rook maneuver.
Bb3 stays on the diagonal guarding g8.
Ra4+ offers the rook while checking the king on a7.
Bxa4 captures that rook but leaves the diagonal to g8.
hxg8=Q captures the black rook and promotes. White’s queen against the remaining bishop is a checked win in this exact position.
branches.explanation: hxg8=Q captures the black rook and promotes. White’s queen against the remaining bishop is a checked win in this exact position.

branches.title: Take the offered rook immediately
commentary: Compare the natural capture before moving the bishop off its useful diagonal.
hxg8=Q captures the rook and creates a queen, but gives away the forced win.
Bxg8 eliminates that queen. White has only Rh4 against Bg8 and the kings; the exact position is drawn with best play.
branches.explanation: Bxg8 eliminates that queen. White has only Rh4 against Bg8 and the kings; the exact position is drawn with best play.

exercises.prompt: Why does Rd4 matter before promotion?
exercises.answer: It attacks the bishop that would recapture on g8. White can then force the king and bishop onto a line where the rook forks them.

exercises.prompt: Why is the same bishop recapture harmless after ...Ka8?
exercises.answer: The king on a8 and bishop on g8 can be forked by Rd8+. Before the king is displaced, that tactic is absent.

startContext: Begin after ...Rg8 at 77 seconds. Earlier rook checks and king placement remain source context. The selected bishop retreats, checking sacrifices, back-rank fork and drawing immediate capture are independently checked.
verification_scope: Saved board images reviewed manually. Every encoded intermediate position and endpoint is checked against the tablebase. Selected instructive variations, not an exhaustive tree of all legal defenses.
